title: The k largest and the running median
objectives: Use a size-k heap and two heaps for top-k and streaming medians.

screens.title: Most traded

screens.question: Tap the three rows the panel shows.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Rank by trades, then break ties by the alphabet.

screens.title: Keep only three
screens.prose: Trade sizes arrive one at a time. To keep the 3 largest, push each size onto a heap. Whenever the heap holds 4, pop its smallest. All ten sizes are pushed.

state.caption: Trade sizes in arrival order, read row by row

screens.question: How many pops happen over the ten trades?

widget.accept: 7: one pop for every push after the third.
widget.label: Pops

hints.text: When does the heap first reach 4?
After the fourth push.
Pushes 4 to 10 each make the heap hold 4, so each causes one pop: 7.

feedback.correct: 10 pushes and 7 pops: the heap ends holding 3.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Every push after the third forces a pop.

byKey.ten: You popped on every push. The first three pushes fill the heap without a pop.
byKey.three: That is how many the heap keeps, not how many it drops.
byKey.six: Count again from push 4 to push 10: that is 7 pushes.

explain.text: The heap grows to 3, then each later push makes it 4 and one pop brings it back. That is $10 - 3 = 7$ pops. In all, $n$ pushes and $n - k$ pops, each $O(\log k)$.

screens.title: Which heap
screens.prose: We keep the 3 largest sizes. After each push we drop one value to get back to 3.

state.caption: Trade sizes in arrival order, read row by row

screens.question: Should the heap be a min-heap or a max-heap?

options.text: A min-heap, so the smallest kept value is on top
A max-heap, so the largest kept value is on top
options.why: Then the top is the value we most want to keep. Popping it throws away the biggest trade.

options.text: Either works, since both pop one value
options.why: They pop different values. Only a min-heap drops the one that no longer belongs.

hints.text: Which of the four values should leave?
The smallest of the four is no longer among the 3 largest.
A min-heap keeps the smallest on top, so `heappop` removes exactly that value.

feedback.correct: The weakest of the kept values sits on top and is the one to drop.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask which value has to leave when the heap holds 4.

byKey.b: You put the best value on top. The heap's top is what gets popped, so it must be the worst.

explain.text: For the $k$ largest, the value to throw away is the smallest kept one. A min-heap keeps it on top. So the top is also the $k$-th largest: here 450, behind 700 and 600.

screens.title: Most frequent words
screens.prose: Return the `k` most frequent words, most frequent first. Words with equal counts come in alphabetical order. Return fewer than `k` if there are fewer distinct words.
screens.question: Write `top_k_frequent(words, k)`.

widget.starter:
import heapq
from collections import Counter

def top_k_frequent(words, k):
    return list(Counter(words))[:k]
widget.solution:
import heapq
from collections import Counter

def top_k_frequent(words, k):
    count = Counter(words)
    best = heapq.nsmallest(k, count.items(),
                           key=lambda kv: (-kv[1], kv[0]))
    return [w for w, _ in best]
widget.how: Check runs 7 hidden tests: ties, `k` above the distinct count, `k = 0`, and 50,000 words with 1,000 distinct. Each result must equal the expected list.

hints.text: What do you compute before any heap?
Count the words, then rank by a two-part key.
`count = Counter(words)`, then `heapq.nsmallest(k, count.items(), key=lambda kv: (-kv[1], kv[0]))` and keep the words.

feedback.correct: Count in $O(n)$, then pick $k$ in $O(m \log k)$ for $m$ distinct words.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the first failing test.

byKey.test-4: Test 4 is a tie: a and b both appear once. Break ties alphabetically.
byKey.test-5: Test 5 ties x and y at 2. Rank by count, then by the word.
byKey.test-7: Test 7 has 1,000 words tied at 50. The first three in the alphabet win.

explain.text: `-kv[1]` makes larger counts sort first, and `kv[0]` breaks ties alphabetically. `nsmallest` keeps a heap of size `k` as it scans the counts. Sorting all the counts would also pass, at $O(m \log m)$.

screens.title: The comparator in C++
screens.prose: `std::priority_queue` keeps the element its comparator ranks highest on top. To keep the best `k`, the top must be the worst of them. So the comparator says `a` is below `b` when `a` is the better entry.

state.caption: The same seven tests as the Python screen

screens.question: Write `top_k_frequent` in C++ with a size-`k` `priority_queue`.

tests.setup: std::vector<std::string> words; for (int i = 0; i < 50000; ++i) words.push_back("w" + std::to_string(10000 + i % 1000).substr(1));

widget.how: The first Check downloads the C++ compiler, about 26 MB, and compiles in 10 to 15 s. Later Checks take 1 to 3 s. Check runs the 7 tests of the Python screen. Each result must equal the expected list.

hints.text: Which entry should `heap.top()` be?
The worst of the kept entries: the lowest count, and on a tie the later word.
`worse(a, b)` returns `a.first > b.first` when counts differ, else `a.second < b.second`. Push, pop above `k`, then read the heap out backwards.

feedback.correct: The comparator puts the worst entry on top, so `pop` drops it.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the first failing test.

byKey.test-1: Test 1 needs `['bid', 'ask']`. The starter's map has no order you can rely on.
byKey.test-4: Test 4 is a tie. On equal counts the later word is worse, so it must sit on top.
byKey.error: The code did not compile or stopped. Check the comparator's types match `Entry`.

explain.text: `priority_queue` pops what its comparator ranks highest. With `worse`, the highest is the lowest count and, on ties, the later word. Popping into `out` from the back gives most frequent first.

screens.title: Ties
screens.prose: A learner ranks by count alone: `sorted(count.items(), key=lambda kv: -kv[1])`. The words are `['bid', 'ask', 'bid', 'ask', 'mid']` and `k = 2`.
screens.question: What should `top_k_frequent` return?

options.why: You sorted by count alone, so the tie kept the order of first appearance. Ties go alphabetically: ask first.
mid appears once, and ask twice. Counts come first.
`k` is 2, so only two words are returned.

hints.text: What is the count of each word?
bid and ask both have 2.
A tie at 2 is broken by the alphabet, so ask comes before bid.

feedback.correct: Count descending, then word ascending: ask, bid.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Rank by count, then break the tie by the word.

byKey.b: You ranked by count only. That leaves ties in dict order, which here is the order of first appearance.

explain.text: Sorting by `-count` alone is stable, so bid stays ahead of ask because it appeared first. A different input order would flip the answer. The key `(-count, word)` makes the result depend on the data alone.

screens.title: The k-th largest of a stream
screens.prose: Start with the numbers in `initial`. After each number in `adds` arrives, record the `k`-th largest of everything so far; the largest is the first. Every call has at least `k` numbers after the first add.
screens.question: Write `kth_largest_stream(k, initial, adds)`.

tests.setup: import random; random.seed(3); xs = [random.randint(0, 10**6) for _ in range(30000)]

widget.how: Check runs 6 hidden tests: an empty start, negatives, repeats and $k = 1$. Test 6 streams 29,000 numbers with $k = 100$ and checks the sum of the answers.

hints.text: Which numbers can still be the $k$-th largest later?
Only the $k$ largest so far. Anything smaller never comes back.
Keep a min-heap of at most `k` numbers. Push each number, pop when it holds `k + 1`, and record `heap[0]` after each add.

feedback.correct: A size-$k$ min-heap answers each add in $O(\log k)$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the first failing test.

byKey.test-1: Test 1 asks for the 3rd largest, not the largest. After adding 6 the three largest are 11, 7 and 6.
byKey.test-4: Test 4 has repeats. Equal values each take a place in the heap.
byKey.test-6: Test 6 timed out or failed. Sorting after every add is too slow; keep the heap of size $k$.

explain.text: A number below the heap's top is pushed and popped at once, and never matters again. The top is the smallest of the $k$ largest, which is the $k$-th largest. Each add costs $O(\log k)$, against $O(n \log n)$ for re-sorting.

screens.title: Two heaps for the median
screens.prose: You built a running median in `ds` homework-4 h4-median. The lower half sits in a max-heap and the upper half in a min-heap. The lower may hold one extra. The median is the lower top, or the mean of both tops.

state.caption: The lower heap may hold one extra value

screens.question: Slide through the values `7, 3, 9, 1, 8, 2`. What do the six running medians add up to?

hints.text: After 7 and 3, what are the two tops?
The lower top is 3 and the upper top is 7, so the median is 5.
The medians are 7, 5, 7, 5, 7, 5, which sum to 36.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. With equal sizes the median is the mean of the two tops.

byKey.tops: With equal sizes you took the upper top. Average the two tops instead.
byKey.last: You may have taken the lower top at every step, or the final median six times. With equal sizes, average the two tops.

explain.text: With an odd count the lower heap is one bigger and its top is the median. With an even count the median is the mean of the two tops. After 6 values the heaps hold 3 and 3; a seventh value would make it 4 and 3.

screens.title: The pattern
screens.prose:
What you wrote, as a pattern:

```python
count = Counter(words)
heap = []                  # worst entry on top
for word, c in count.items():
    push (c, word) ranked worst first
    if len(heap) > k: pop the worst
return the k entries, best first
```
screens.question: Put the steps of top-`k` by frequency in order. Leave out the step that does not belong.

lines.text: Count each word with a dict
Push each (count, word) entry onto a heap with the worst entry on top
Pop the worst entry whenever the heap holds k + 1
Pop the k survivors and reverse them, best first
Pop the worst entry whenever the heap holds k
lines.why: Then the heap keeps only k − 1 entries after each pop, and the k-th best is lost.

feedback.correct: Count, push, pop above $k$, read out.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. The heap may reach $k + 1$ for a moment before the pop.

byKey.d1: You popped at size `k`. That leaves $k - 1$, one short of the answer.
byKey.left-out: Every step but one belongs. Only popping at size `k` is wrong.

explain.text: Counting first turns words into entries with a rank. The heap of size $k$ holds the best so far with the worst on top, ready to drop. Reading it out gives worst first, so reverse it.

screens.title: A median over the last 500,000 trades
screens.prose: A risk screen shows the median size of the last 500,000 trades and updates on every trade. Each new trade enters the window and the oldest leaves.

state.caption: The lower heap may hold one extra value

screens.question: Which structure fits best?

options.text: Two heaps with lazy deletion of the leaving trades
A sorted list rebuilt from the 500,000 trades on every update
options.why: That sorts 500,000 values per trade, about 9.5 million steps, $O(w \log w)$ each time. The heaps do $O(\log w)$.
One heap gives only the smallest value. The median needs both halves.

options.text: Two heaps that simply ignore leaving trades
options.why: Then old trades stay in the halves and the median drifts away from the last 500,000.

hints.text: What is new compared with the running median?
A trade also leaves the window on every update.
Keep two heaps, and on removal note the value; pop it later when it surfaces at a top.

feedback.correct: Two heaps, with removals done lazily when a marked value reaches a top.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. The window both grows and shrinks on each trade.

byKey.b: You rebuild everything per trade. That works, but at 500,000 values it costs far more than two heap operations.

explain.text: A heap cannot delete from its middle cheaply. So we count the leaving value as pending and pop it when it reaches a top. The homework item `window_median` asks you to write it.

screens.title: Re-sort or keep a heap
screens.prose: A screen shows the 10 largest of $n = 100{,}000$ trade sizes. One way re-sorts all of them when a new trade size arrives, about $n \log n$ work. The other keeps a size-10 heap, about $\log k$ work per arrival with $k = 10$.

state.caption: Trade sizes in arrival order, read row by row

screens.question: About how many times more work per update does re-sorting do?

hints.text: Is the base of the logarithm important in a ratio?
No: $\tfrac{\log 100{,}000}{\log 10} = 5$ in any base.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide $n \log n$ by $\log k$.

byKey.nologk: That is $n \log_2 n$ alone. Divide by the heap's $\log_2 10 \approx 3.32$.
byKey.nk: That is $n / k$. The work per update is $n \log n$ against $\log k$.
byKey.n: You dropped the logarithms. Their ratio is 5, not 1.

explain.text: $\tfrac{\log 100{,}000}{\log 10} = 5$, whatever the base. So the ratio is $100{,}000 \times 5 = 500{,}000$. The heap also needs only 10 slots of memory.

ideas: To keep the $k$ largest, hold a min-heap of size $k$ and pop whenever it grows to $k + 1$. Its top is the $k$-th largest.
To rank by frequency, count first, then rank by the key `(-count, word)` so ties break alphabetically.
In C++, `priority_queue` pops what its comparator ranks highest. So a heap of the best $k$ needs the worst entry on top.
summary.trap: Ranking by count alone leaves ties in input order, so the answer changes when the input is shuffled.

options.why: You kept the word that appeared first. On a tie the alphabet decides, and buy comes first.
`k` is 1, so one word is returned.

feedback.correct: Both appear twice; buy is earlier in the alphabet.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Break the tie by the word.

explain.text: sell and buy both have count 2. The key `(-count, word)` puts buy first. So the answer is `['buy']`.

quiz.prose: Twelve values stream into a heap that keeps the 4 largest: push each, and pop when it holds 5.
quiz.question: How many pops happen?

widget.accept: 8: one pop for each push after the fourth.
widget.label: Pops

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The first four pushes need no pop.

byKey.twelve: The first four pushes fill the heap without a pop.
byKey.four: That is what the heap keeps. Count what it drops.

quiz.prose: We want the 5 largest of a long stream, with memory for only 5 numbers.
quiz.question: What do we keep?

options.why: Its top is the largest, so a pop would drop the best value.

options.text: A max-heap of every number, popped 5 times at the end
options.why: That gives the right answer but stores the whole stream, not 5 numbers.

options.text: A sorted list of every number
options.why: That stores the whole stream as well.

feedback.correct: The smallest kept value is on top, ready to be dropped.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. The memory limit rules out storing the stream.

explain.text: A min-heap of size 5 holds the 5 largest so far. Its top is the 5th largest, the first to go when a bigger value arrives. Memory stays at 5.

quiz.question: What is `q.top()`?

options.why: The default comparator, `std::less`, puts the largest on top. `std::greater` reverses it.
`top()` is not the first value pushed. It is the value the comparator ranks highest.
3 is neither end. The heap's top is an extreme value.

feedback.correct: `std::greater` makes it a min-heap: the top is 1.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Which value does `std::greater` rank highest?

explain.text: `priority_queue` puts on top the element that no other ranks above. With `std::greater`, a larger value ranks lower, so the smallest is on top. A size-$k$ heap of the $k$ largest uses exactly this.
